title: Syntax and Variables
summary: The building blocks of every C program: statements, blocks, comments and case-sensitive names, plus how to declare, initialise and scope variables and constants.
introduction: Before you can express an idea in C you need its grammar: where semicolons go, what braces mean, how comments work and how variables are declared. C is strict about all of this and the compiler rejects programs that break the rules, which is good news because the rules are few. This lesson covers the shape of a program, variable declarations and initialisation, naming conventions, constants, and the block scope that decides where a name is visible.
learningObjectives: Write syntactically correct statements, blocks and comments
Declare, initialise and assign variables of the basic types
Define constants with const, #define and enum
Predict which variable a name refers to using block scope

blocks.text: The shape of a C program

A C program is a sequence of **declarations** and **statements**. A declaration introduces a name (a variable, a function, a type); a statement does something. Every simple statement ends with a semicolon, and braces group statements into a **block** that counts as a single statement. Line breaks and indentation carry no meaning: the compiler sees `int x = 1; int y = 2;` on one line exactly as it sees them on two. Names are case-sensitive, so `total`, `Total` and `TOTAL` are three different variables.

blocks.title: shape.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 shape.c -o shape
$ ./shape
Area: 12
That is a big rectangle.

items: `/* ... */` comments may span several lines but cannot be nested; `// ...` comments (standard since C99) run to the end of the line.
Lines beginning with `#` are preprocessor directives, handled before compilation proper, and take no semicolon.
A block `{ ... }` may appear wherever a statement may, and every `if`, loop and function body is one.

blocks.text: A variable is a named piece of memory with a **type**. The type fixes how many bytes the variable occupies and how its bits are interpreted, and it never changes. Declare with `type name;` or, better, `type name = value;`. Several variables of one type may share a declaration, and since C99 a declaration may appear anywhere a statement can, not only at the top of a block. The [next lesson](/tutorials/c/data-types) looks at each type in depth; here you only need `int` for whole numbers, `double` for fractional numbers and `char` for single characters.

blocks.title: variables.c

rows: Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter
Valid; all-caps is conventionally reserved for macros and constants
Names starting with an underscore are reserved for the compiler and library in many contexts
A name cannot start with a digit
The hyphen is the minus operator: this is `first` minus `name`
Keywords such as `int`, `if`, `return` and `sizeof` cannot be reused

blocks.text: Most C code uses `snake_case` for variables and functions, and names that say what the value *means* (`row_count`, not `rc`). Single letters are fine for loop counters and coordinates.

A local variable declared without an initialiser holds whatever bits happened to be in that memory, an **indeterminate value**. Reading it is a bug, and frequently undefined behaviour, that produces different results on different runs or compilers. The compiler catches many cases when warnings are on:

blocks.title: uninit.c
Terminal (GCC 13; wording differs between versions)
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 uninit.c -o uninit
uninit.c: In function 'main':
uninit.c:8:11: warning: 'total' is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]
    8 |     total = total + bonus;
      |     ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

blocks.text: The program still builds and prints some number, which is exactly the problem: it may print 5 on your machine and 32773 on a colleague's. The fix is to write `int total = 0;`. Make it a rule to give every variable a value in its declaration unless you assign one on the very next line.

C has three ways to name a value that never changes, and they are not interchangeable. A `const` variable is a real variable that the compiler refuses to assign to; it has a type and a scope. A `#define` macro is textual replacement performed by the preprocessor before compilation: it has no type and ignores scope. An `enum` constant is a genuine integer constant that may be used anywhere the compiler needs a value at compile time, such as an array size. C23 adds `constexpr` for typed compile-time constants, but in C17 these three are what you have.

blocks.title: constants.c

blocks.text: Scope: where a name is visible

A variable declared inside a block exists from its declaration to the block's closing brace: that is **block scope**. A variable declared outside every function has **file scope** and is visible from its declaration to the end of the file. An inner block may declare a variable with the same name as an outer one; the inner one *shadows* the outer one until the block ends. Shadowing compiles, but it confuses readers, and the `-Wshadow` flag reports it.

blocks.title: scope.c
Common mistake: double quotes for a character
blocks.text: `char grade = "B";` is wrong even though it may compile with a warning. `'B'` in single quotes is one character, the number 66. `"B"` in double quotes is a *string*: two bytes, the letter and a terminating zero, and the expression is the address of that string, not a character. Use single quotes for one character and double quotes for text.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Compile `scope.c` with `-Wshadow` added to the usual flags and read the warning about `value`. Then move `int i` out of the `for` header and declare it before the loop; `i` is now visible after the loop too, which is sometimes exactly what you want.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid C variable name?
questions.explanation: Names consist of letters, digits and underscores and cannot start with a digit; `first-name` is a subtraction and `int` is a keyword.

questions.question: A local variable declared without an initialiser, such as `int n;`, starts at 0.
questions.explanation: Only variables with static storage (file scope or `static`) start at zero. A plain local variable holds an indeterminate value until you assign one.
